subject: Science
title: Friction depends on the job
objective: Explain when friction helps and when it hinders.
recall: Name a push or a pull.
Point to two surfaces touching in the model.
starter: A brake pad presses against a turning wheel. Would less friction help it stop?
starter_answer: No. Friction between the pad and wheel resists their relative sliding and slows the wheel.
model: Friction is a contact force between surfaces that slide, or try to slide, past each other.
The force opposes that relative sliding. The effect depends on the pair of surfaces.
Grip can be helpful; unwanted heating and wear can be a problem.
hinge: A: Friction only acts on rough surfaces.
B: Smooth surfaces can also have friction.
C: Friction is always unwanted.
hinge_answer: B. Smooth surfaces can still grip. Name the two surfaces and the job before judging the effect.
connect: On a moving box, draw friction opposite its sliding along the floor.
On a stationary shoe, friction can prevent slipping.
A smooth-looking surface is not enough evidence to predict every surface pair.

activity.title: Choose the job, then judge the force
activity.prompt: Sort these situations into helpful, unhelpful or need more information. Defend one choice.
items: A: Brake pad rubbing a bicycle wheel.
B: Machine parts heating and wearing as they rub.
C: A handle gripping a hand.
D: Two unknown materials touching.
activity.answer: A helps braking; B can waste energy and damage parts; C helps grip. D needs the intended job and the surface pair. There is no single good/bad label for friction.

independent: Draw a box sliding right. Add a friction arrow. Explain one helpful and one unhelpful example using the two touching surfaces.
model_answer: The friction arrow on the sliding box points left. Pad–wheel friction helps braking. Friction between moving machine parts can heat and wear them; reducing this friction can be useful.
exit_question: What information do you need before saying friction is helpful?
exit_answer: The touching surfaces, the relative motion or attempted sliding, and the intended job.
prep: Print the worksheet. Use a still model or an adult demonstration with a low ramp and a light sliding block. Hand rubbing is optional; no heat or flame demonstration.
trap: Avoid “friction always opposes an object’s travel” as a universal rule. It opposes relative slipping at a contact; static friction can help us walk forwards.
support: Point to the surfaces, then finish: “Resisting sliding helps this job because …”.
source_note: School GROW Science SoW and the current matching lesson. White Rose Education Year 5 Autumn Block 1, user upload, informs W3–W5. W6–W7 retain the school sequence.

subject: Science
title: Compare two sliding surfaces
objective: Use repeated observations to compare friction in one setup.
recall: Name the force between sliding surfaces.
Give one job where grip helps.
starter: We change both the block and the surface. Can stopping distance tell us which surface caused the difference?
starter_answer: No. Changing the block as well as the surface leaves more than one possible cause.
model: Keep the same block, low ramp, release mark and no-push release. Change the run-out surface.
Measure from the same zero to the same edge of the stopped block, in centimetres.
Repeat each surface. Keep the first results even if they differ.
hinge: A: Push harder on the rough surface.
B: Change only the run-out surface.
C: Choose a different block for each surface.
hinge_answer: B. Keeping the other setup choices the same makes the surface comparison more useful.
connect: A shorter slide can support greater resistance in this particular setup.
Compare repeated values, not just the run that fits your prediction.
A result with a known release mistake needs a note and a retry; keep its record.

activity.title: Check the evidence
activity.prompt: Invented teaching data from the same sliding-block setup. Compare both trials before making a claim.
items: Which surface stopped the block sooner in both trials?
What must have stayed the same for this to be a useful comparison?
activity.answer: B stopped it sooner in both trials. The evidence supports greater resistance on B in this setup, if the block, ramp, release and measuring method were controlled. These are supplied data, not measurements made by this class.

exit_question: Why should we keep a surprising result?
exit_answer: It is part of the evidence. We can flag uncertainty, check the method and repeat without silently deleting it.

subject: Science
title: Levers, pulleys and gears
objective: Identify three mechanisms and explain what each changes.
recall: What is a force?
Where do the blades of scissors turn?
starter: A fixed wheel at the top of a flagpole changes the direction of the pull. Does it automatically halve the effort?
starter_answer: No. A single ideal fixed pulley changes the pull direction; it does not by itself halve the effort.
model: A lever is a rigid bar turning around a pivot. Mark the effort and the load.
A fixed pulley can let a downward pull lift a load upwards.
Meshing gears have teeth that transmit turning. Different sizes trade turning speed and turning force.
hinge: A: A mechanism creates extra energy.
B: Every pulley reduces effort by half.
C: A mechanism can change force size or direction.
hinge_answer: C. The gain depends on the arrangement. No mechanism gives extra energy for free.
connect: For the same load, a longer effort arm on a lever can reduce the effort needed.
The effort then moves through a greater distance for the same load rise.
For meshing gears, a smaller driven gear turns faster but supplies less turning force in an ideal system.

activity.title: Mechanism detective
activity.prompt: Match each example to a mechanism, then give the deciding feature.
items: A: A seesaw turning on its middle support.
B: A rope over a fixed wheel lifting a flag.
C: Two toothed wheels turning together.
activity.answer: A is a lever: a bar turns around a pivot. B is a pulley: the rope passes over a wheel and changes pull direction. C uses gears: the teeth transmit rotation. A name alone does not explain the effect.

independent: Sketch and label a lever’s pivot, effort and load. Explain one change made by a fixed pulley or a pair of gears.
model_answer: A lever turns around the pivot; effort is applied to lift or move the load. A single fixed pulley changes the direction of the pull. Meshing gears turn in opposite directions and can change turning speed and turning force.
exit_question: What should you ask when a mechanism makes a task feel easier?
exit_answer: What changed, what stayed the same, and whether the effort must travel farther or the output moves more slowly.
prep: Use the labelled diagram and an adult-held ruler lever with a light secured load. Keep fingers away from any moving gear teeth or pulley. Do not open paint tins or use pupils as seesaw loads.
trap: The inherited wording can imply greater force and greater speed together. Explain the trade-off and distinguish fixed pulleys from pulley systems.
support: Look for a bar and pivot, a rope and wheel, or teeth. Point before naming.
source_note: School GROW Science SoW and the current matching lesson. White Rose Education Year 5 Autumn Block 1, user upload, informs W3–W5. W6–W7 retain the school sequence.

subject: Science
title: Move the pivot, compare the effort
objective: Compare two lever arrangements while keeping the load the same.
recall: Point to a pivot.
Does a mechanism create energy?
starter: The load changes from one trial to the next. Can we judge the effect of moving the pivot?
starter_answer: Not fairly: the load has also changed. Keep the same load when comparing pivot positions.
model: Mark one effort point and two pivot positions. Keep the same light load.
Lift the load through the same small height. Compare how much effort is needed.
Observe how far the effort point moves. Easier can mean farther.
hinge: A: Move the pivot nearer the load and keep the load rise fixed.
B: Use a lighter load in the second trial.
C: Push from an unmarked position each time.
hinge_answer: A gives a more useful comparison of pivot position. B and C introduce other changes.
connect: A longer effort arm relative to the load arm can reduce the needed effort.
Use easier/similar/harder only as a qualitative observation.
Write a force in newtons only if it was measured with a suitable force meter.

activity.title: Predict a gear pair
activity.prompt: Two meshing gears have 20 and 40 teeth. The 40-tooth gear makes one complete turn.
items: How many turns must the 20-tooth gear make?
Do meshing gears turn in the same or opposite directions?
What does this model leave out?
activity.answer: The 20-tooth gear makes two turns in the opposite direction: 40 teeth pass the contact point. This ideal model leaves out friction and deformation. It does not mean the smaller gear supplies both more speed and more turning force.

independent: Compare the two prepared lever positions, or explain them from the diagram. Record the same load, the pivot position and the observed effort. Explain the gain and the cost.
model_answer: With the pivot nearer the load and a longer effort arm, less effort is needed for the same load, but the effort point travels farther for the same load rise. A diagram explanation is modelling; only record observations if a comparison was actually made.
exit_question: Why must the load rise be the same in both comparisons?
exit_answer: It lets us compare the effort movement needed to achieve the same lift, rather than two different jobs.
prep: Prepare a stable ruler lever, non-rolling pivot and small secured load close to the table. Mark the effort point and a small target lift. Use the still comparison when practical work is unavailable.
trap: A qualitative comparison is not a measured force. Do not add invented newtons to a result table.
support: Use: “The pivot is closer to … . I noticed … . For the same lift, the hand moves …”.
source_note: School GROW Science SoW and the current matching lesson. White Rose Education Year 5 Autumn Block 1, user upload, informs W3–W5. W6–W7 retain the school sequence.

subject: Science
title: Plan a test we can trust
objective: Plan a fair test of run-out surface and stopping distance.
recall: What did we keep the same in the sliding-block comparison?
What unit did we use for distance?
starter: Two trolley runs have different surfaces and different pushes. Which change caused the longer distance?
starter_answer: The evidence cannot separate the causes. We need a controlled release and one planned variable change.
model: Question: does the run-out surface affect how far the same trolley rolls?
Change the surface. Measure stopping distance in centimetres.
Keep the trolley, ramp height, release point and no-push release the same.
hinge: A: The stopping distance is what we measure.
B: The stopping distance must be fixed.
C: We change the trolley for every surface.
hinge_answer: A. Distance is the dependent variable. The surface is the independent variable; the other planned conditions are controls.
connect: Write the plan before using equipment. Label the ruler zero.
Repeat each surface using the same measuring point on the trolley.
A test can be controlled even when people take different roles. “Fair” here describes the comparison.

activity.title: Repair the plan
activity.prompt: Choose the first changes needed to make this method useful.
items: “Use two different trolleys.”
“Push until it feels fast.”
“Measure from wherever the ruler starts.”
“Keep only the longest result.”
activity.answer: Use the same trolley and a fixed no-push release. Measure from a marked zero to the same trolley edge. Keep and compare repeated results, noting mistakes. Changing several things prevents a clear causal conclusion.

independent: Complete a plan with the question, CHANGE, MEASURE with unit, at least two controls and three repeats per surface. Sketch the starting mark and measuring zero.
model_answer: Question: does run-out surface affect stopping distance? CHANGE: surface. MEASURE: stopping distance/cm. KEEP: trolley, ramp height, release point, no push and the measuring method. Run three trials on each surface and keep every result.
exit_question: What is the difference between a control variable and a measured variable?
exit_answer: We deliberately keep a control the same; the measured variable is the result we record.
prep: Prepare planning cards and a drawing of the secured setup. Demonstrate a no-push release if suitable. Tuesday uses the same plan; save each pupil’s first version and agreed correction.
trap: Repeats do not repair an unfair method. A clear question and controls come first.
support: Use the three headings CHANGE / KEEP / MEASURE. Give one item under each before extending.
source_note: School GROW Science SoW and the current matching lesson. White Rose Education Year 5 Autumn Block 1, user upload, informs W3–W5. W6–W7 retain the school sequence.

subject: Science
title: Run, record and evaluate
objective: Use repeated evidence to answer a forces question and explain a limitation.
recall: State the one planned change.
Point to one control in your plan.
starter: One run was pushed accidentally. Should we erase it so the results look tidy?
starter_answer: No. Keep it, label the known method problem and repeat if possible. The record should show why the repeat was needed.
model: Check the setup and agree tester, director, observer or recorder roles.
Take three no-push releases per surface when practicable, recording centimetres each time.
Compare the results, retain uncertainty and conclude only what the evidence supports.
hinge: A: Delete a result that disagrees.
B: Keep it, flag the concern and check the method.
C: Change the numbers to fit the prediction.
hinge_answer: B. A surprising value is evidence to investigate, not a reason to invent or remove results.
connect: A mean summarises repeated values: add them and divide by the number of trials.
A mean does not remove a faulty method or prove the result true.
Separate what the values show from what we assume about the setup.

activity.title: Evidence conference
activity.prompt: Invented teaching data, available when practical work cannot run. Compare the two surfaces.
items: Calculate the two means if ready.
Choose a supported conclusion and one limitation.
activity.answer: Mean A = (48 + 50 + 49) ÷ 3 = 49 cm. Mean B = 28 cm. The trolley stopped over a shorter distance on B in these sample data. We need assurance that release and measurement were controlled. This analysis is not a practical the class completed.

independent: Use your actual results, or label the provided sample-data route. Record a conclusion with two values, one uncertainty and one method improvement. Keep the original evidence.
model_answer: Sample model: B has a mean of 28 cm compared with A’s 49 cm, so the trolley rolled a shorter distance on B in this setup. The conclusion depends on a controlled release. A fixed release mark and no push would improve consistency. Practical conclusions must follow the actual retained measurements.
exit_question: What does your evidence support—and what can it not establish?
exit_answer: It can support a comparison for the tested setup. It cannot establish every surface pair, and sample values do not establish practical completion.
prep: Use Monday’s approved plan, a secured low ramp, the same trolley, two surfaces, tape and padded stop. Run the hands-on work during shared and independent stages. If no suitable setup, use the clearly labelled sample data throughout. Keep a known pushed trial in the record, label it invalid for the intended comparison, and state which valid trials were used in any mean.
trap: Keep real measurements and supplied values in separate tables. Do not paste sample numbers into a practical record.
support: Compare one A value with one B value first. Say “In these results … because …”.

subject: Science
title: Put the planets in order
objective: Describe the Earth and other planets orbiting the Sun.
recall: Name our planet.
Name the star at the centre of our Solar System.
starter: Does “there is no gravity in space” explain why Earth stays in its orbit?
starter_answer: No. Gravity acts in space. The Sun’s gravitational pull continually changes the direction of Earth’s motion.
model: The eight planets orbit the Sun. Earth is the third planet from it.
Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the inner rocky planets.
Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.
hinge: A: Earth orbits the Sun.
B: The Sun orbits Earth once each day.
C: All planets take one Earth year to orbit.
hinge_answer: A. A planet’s year is the time it takes to complete one orbit; the planets have different year lengths.
connect: Draw a gravity arrow from Earth towards the Sun.
Draw a motion arrow along the path, not directly away from the Sun.
An orbit is a curved path. Classroom drawings simplify its size and shape.

activity.title: Build the order together
activity.prompt: Arrange the planet names from the Sun outwards, then explain one placement.
items: Neptune · Earth · Mercury · Jupiter
Venus · Saturn · Mars · Uranus
activity.answer: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. The first four are rocky planets. The diagram’s gaps and planet sizes are not to scale.

independent: Order the eight planets, or the inner four with the remaining names provided. Add a Sun–Earth sketch with a gravity arrow and explain what an orbit is.
model_answer: Earth is third from the Sun. An orbit is the curved path an object follows around another. The Sun’s gravity pulls inward while Earth keeps moving along its path; the pull changes the motion’s direction.
exit_question: What does the inward arrow represent?
exit_answer: The Sun’s gravitational force on Earth, directed towards the Sun.
prep: Print the name cards and use counters or pointing. Public walking is optional. Use the still diagram; do not look at the Sun. The missing uploaded Block 2 is not assumed to have been reviewed.
trap: Do not draw an outward “motion force” balancing gravity. Motion is along the path; gravity changes its direction.
support: Start Sun → Mercury → Venus → Earth → Mars. Use an arrow from Earth towards the Sun.
source_note: School GROW Science SoW and the current matching lesson. White Rose Education Year 5 Autumn Block 1, user upload, informs W3–W5. W6–W7 retain the school sequence.

questions.answer: No. Gravity acts in space. The Sun’s gravitational pull continually changes the direction of Earth’s motion.

questions.prompt: Arrange the planet names from the Sun outwards, then explain one placement.
questions.answer: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. The first four are rocky planets. The diagram’s gaps and planet sizes are not to scale.

questions.prompt: Order the eight planets, or the inner four with the remaining names provided. Add a Sun–Earth sketch with a gravity arrow and explain what an orbit is.
questions.answer: Earth is third from the Sun. An orbit is the curved path an object follows around another. The Sun’s gravity pulls inward while Earth keeps moving along its path; the pull changes the motion’s direction.

title: Use a model, name its limits
objective: Use a model and year data to explain planetary motion.
recall: Which planet is third from the Sun?

starter: If gravity stopped acting in our simple orbit model, would Earth head directly outwards from the Sun?

model: Move an Earth counter around a Sun counter. Keep an inward gravity arrow.

hinge: A: A model’s planet sizes must be real sizes.
B: A model can explain one feature while simplifying others.

hinge_answer: B. State what the model shows and what it leaves out.
connect: An Earth year is about 365 days; a Mars year is about 687 Earth days.
Compare the stated values before predicting a pattern.

activity.title: Test a year-length claim
activity.prompt: Approximate orbital periods in Earth days. Which comparisons support “farther out, longer year” for these planets?
items: Compare Earth with Mars.
Why is a single hand-made orbit not enough evidence to measure a year?
activity.answer: Mars takes about 322 more Earth days than Earth (687 − 365). Mercury’s 88 days is shorter than Earth’s year. The reference values support the stated pattern for these examples; hand speed in a counter model is chosen by us.
activity.table_caption: Approximate reference values, not class measurements

independent: Draw a two-arrow orbit model and use two values from the table to explain a year-length comparison. Add one limitation of your model.
model_answer: Gravity points towards the Sun; motion is along the curved path. Mars’s year is about 687 Earth days, longer than Earth’s 365. A counter model does not show real scale or orbital speed, and our hand is moving it.
exit_question: How can a model be useful and still have a limitation?
exit_answer: It can make a relationship clear while simplifying other features. Naming the limitation prevents an unsupported claim.
prep: Provide two counters, two arrow cards and the year table. Use drawing, directing or speaking. No strings, swinging masses or public movement are needed.
trap: Near-circular is a simplification, not a claim that all orbits are perfect circles.
support: Use “The model shows … . It does not show …”. Compare 687 with 365.

subject: Science
title: Explain the changing Moon view
objective: Explain ordinary Moon phases using reflected sunlight.
recall: What does “orbit” mean?
Does the Moon make its own visible light?
starter: Is Earth’s shadow the cause of the ordinary monthly Moon phases?
starter_answer: No. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of its sunlit half. Earth’s shadow matters in a lunar eclipse.
model: The Moon is Earth’s natural satellite and reflects sunlight.
In the ordinary phase model, sunlight lights half the Moon.
Our view of that lit half changes as the Moon moves around Earth.
hinge: A: The Moon changes its physical shape.
B: We see different amounts of its sunlit half.
C: The Sun switches the Moon’s light on and off.
hinge_answer: B. The Moon remains a sphere while the visible sunlit portion changes.
connect: Near the Sun’s direction we see the new-Moon view. Do not look at the Sun.
At a side position we see a half-Moon view.
Opposite the Sun’s direction we see the full-Moon view; ordinary phases are not eclipses.

activity.title: Repair the Moon claims
activity.prompt: Choose a claim to repair. Use the still model to explain your correction.
items: “The Moon glows by itself.”
“It becomes a different shape every week.”
“It can only be seen at night.”
activity.answer: The Moon reflects sunlight. It remains round; the amount of its sunlit half visible from Earth changes. It can sometimes be seen during the day. No solar observation is required for this lesson.

independent: Draw three equal circles showing new, half and full Moon views. Explain why the lit part we can see changes.
model_answer: The three circles remain the same shape. Shade almost all for new, half for the half-Moon view and none for full. As the Moon orbits Earth, our viewing angle changes, so we see different amounts of the sunlit half.
exit_question: What changes during an ordinary phase cycle: the Moon’s shape or our view?
exit_answer: Our view of its sunlit half changes; the Moon stays round.
prep: Use the embedded still model and circle cards. Optional adult-held low-power torch and ball, with normal room light and no beam in eyes. Agree any light-level change; no blackout, laser or Sun viewing.
trap: Keep phases separate from eclipses. “Half is lit” describes the ordinary sunlight model; an eclipse is a different alignment.
support: Point to the lit part that the observer can see. Finish “We see … because …”.

subject: Science
title: Test and improve a Moon model
objective: Use a model to check three Moon views and explain its limits.
recall: What lights the Moon?
Name two views from the ordinary phase cycle.
starter: A torch-and-ball model puts the ball in your head’s shadow. Does that show an ordinary Moon phase?
starter_answer: No. That blocks the light and models an eclipse-like shadow. Keep the ball slightly above the head’s shadow when modelling ordinary phases.
model: Keep the light direction fixed and choose one observer position.
Check the new, side and full views with a ball or still diagram.
Keep the Moon round in every drawing. Change the portion shown lit.
hinge: A: Change the light direction each time to get a preferred picture.
B: Keep the light fixed and change the Moon position.
C: Cut a new-shaped ball for each phase.
hinge_answer: B. Position and viewing angle explain the ordinary changing view.
connect: One orbit relative to the stars takes about 27.3 days.
A new-Moon-to-new-Moon phase cycle takes about 29.5 days.
Both are roughly a month, but they describe different repeating relationships.

activity.title: Choose the right explanation
activity.prompt: Match each observation with the relevant idea, then improve one sentence.
items: A: A crescent becomes a half-Moon view.
B: Earth’s shadow crosses the Moon in a lunar eclipse.
C: The Moon keeps nearly the same face towards Earth.
activity.answer: A: changing view of the sunlit half during the orbit. B: Earth blocks sunlight in the eclipse alignment. C: the Moon rotates once for each orbit. Ordinary phases are not the Earth’s shadow.

independent: Check three model views, record one correction and explain a limitation. Use the two period values to distinguish an orbit from a phase cycle if ready.
model_answer: Model answer: I corrected the half-Moon drawing so the circle stayed round and only half the visible face was lit. The torch-and-ball model helps show the changing view, but its distances and sizes are not to scale. About 27.3 days describes an orbit; about 29.5 days describes the repeating phase cycle.
exit_question: What correction made your explanation more accurate?
exit_answer: Accept a specific change supported by the model, such as separating changing view from changing shape or distinguishing a phase from an eclipse.
prep: Keep Monday’s cards. Offer three-view drawing or directing an adult’s model. Restore room conditions promptly. The NASA video is optional; the same question can be answered using the still model.
trap: A model observation is not a measurement of the Moon’s real orbital period.
support: Say what you first thought, point to the model evidence, then change one part of the same explanation.
